query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy alloys (HEAs), toughness retention is governed by the stability and local morphology of phase and grain boundaries that mediate inelastic energy dissipation via transformation‐induced mechanisms. In particular, if grain boundaries are engineered to adopt a serrated (or undulated) morphology through modified cooling/aging protocols, then they will favor dynamic local deformation (such as crystalline-to-amorphous phase transformation and the formation of nanobridges) that blunts cracks and minimizes strain localization, thereby retaining toughness even under high-temperature or high-strain‐rate conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase or dual-phase HEA (e.g., a Ti–Nb–Ta–Zr–Mo or CrMnFeCoNi alloy) with conventionally processed (fast cooled) microstructure exhibiting relatively straight grain (or phase) boundaries.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled heat-treatment protocol that reduces the cooling rate after solution treatment so as to induce controlled grain boundary serration and coarsening of nano-precipitates at the boundaries.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted over a range of temperatures (e.g., room temperature to 700°C) and strain rates typical for demanding engineering applications; the alloy composition is maintained in the regime where ductility loss by intergranular cracking previously occurs.
generation.structural_mediator: Engineered serrated grain boundaries and associated nano-scale precipitates or stabilized phase boundaries that promote local transformation (e.g., dislocation-mediated crystalline-to-amorphous transition or nanobridge formation) at the crack tip.
generation.mechanism: The serrated boundaries reduce local stress concentration by distributing strains more evenly across the interface, which in turn delays crack initiation. Under deformation, these boundaries facilitate a local phase transformation (such as amorphization or formation of nanobridges) that absorbs energy and blunts crack propagation. This mechanism suppresses the deleterious effects of fast elemental segregation (which otherwise lowers interfacial cohesion) and promotes a synergy of dislocation plasticity and transformation-induced toughening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline with straight boundaries, the alloy with serrated (engineered) boundaries should exhibit increased tensile fracture strain, prolonged creep rupture life (e.g., improvements by factors comparable to or exceeding those previously reported, such as a 3.5× increase in tensile ductility and a several-hundred-fold improvement in creep rupture life under comparable conditions), and a delay in the onset of intergranular cracking. These effects will be most pronounced in temperature regimes where conventional processing leads to ductility drop.
generation.baseline: The as-received or fast-cooled HEA featuring straight grain boundaries that, at elevated temperatures, suffer from localized strain concentration and associated intergranular cracking resulting in toughness loss.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis should hold for multi-principal element alloys (HEAs/MPEAs) with similar phase compositions (e.g., fcc or dual-phase alloys based on Ti–Nb–Ta–Zr–Mo or CrMnFeCoNi systems) processed under conditions that yield comparable grain sizes and when tested in temperature and strain-rate regimes that are known to trigger ductility loss through grain boundary decohesion or rapid segregation.
generation.uncertainty: The proposed mechanism builds on evidence reporting transformation-induced nanobridge toughening in CrMnFeCoNi (PMC8011962) and the demonstration of enhanced ductility via serrated grain boundaries in a precipitation-strengthened HEA (PMC9848264), as well as phase-boundary–mediated strain localization mitigation (PMC12061292). What is new in this proposal is the hypothesis that controlled grain boundary serration not only improves ductility but actively promotes localized phase transformations (e.g., formation of amorphous interlayers or nanobridges) that serve as intrinsic/extrinsic toughening mechanisms. The extent of the beneficial transformation and its sensitivity to processing parameters remain to be precisely quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the same HEA composition. Process one set with a fast cooling rate to obtain straight grain boundaries (baseline) and the other set with a reduced cooling rate or modified aging that yields serrated boundaries. Perform tensile and creep tests at various temperatures (e.g., room temperature and 650°C) while monitoring crack initiation and propagation via in situ electron microscopy.
measurements: Quantitative fracture toughness (KJIc) and tensile ductility (fracture strain)
Creep rupture life under controlled stress at elevated temperature
Grain boundary morphology characterization (via SEM/TEM) and in situ observation of local deformation (nanobridge or phase transformation formation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the engineered (serrated) grain boundary samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in toughness, ductility, or delayed crack initiation relative to the baseline samples under equivalent testing conditions—or if in situ microscopy fails to reveal the expected localized transformation mechanisms at the boundaries—then the hypothesis that serrated boundaries mediate toughness retention via transformation-induced energy dissipation would be falsified.

In contrast to single-phase samples (Fig. 3D), the dual-phase sample has very few cracks near the lateral fracture surface. This suggests that the GB segregation engineering strategy via preexisting Cr-rich precipitates is effective to evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures in HEAs. This is because the embrittling elements—such as Cr, Mn, or Ni—can be absorbed by preexisting embrittling element–enriched precipitates at GBs, which only leads to the growth of precipitates rather than GB embrittlement. While strength and ductility are the global mechanical properties controlled by their bulk responses, fracture toughness originates from the resistance to crack initiation and propagation that is more closely related to the local microstructure and evolution. Therefore, the near-tip mechanisms revealed in this work, including the crystalline-to-amorphous phase transformation and formation of amorphous nanobridges, could be generally applicable to the toughening of other UFG HEAs. In conclusion, we have found the deformation-induced crystalline-to-amorphous phase transformation in the UFG Cantor alloy. The structural evolution exhibits a sequence of formation of the crystalline, lamellar, spotted, and amorphous patterns in TEM images that arise from different proportions and organizations of the crystalline and amorphous structures. The crack-tip high stresses, high lattice and grain boundary resistances to dislocation slip, and resulting accumulation of high-density dislocations are essential to the observed solid-state amorphization, thereby dissipating energy and resisting crack propagation. ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology.
